|❶|**语义降维 (Semantic Shredding)**：把知识切碎成浮点数向量，丢失了原始的层级结构、因果关系和优先级|AI 检索到的是碎片，不是知识|
|❷|**只读架构 (Read-Only by Design)**：RAG 本质是静态文档库——AI 能"查"，但不能"写回"、"修正"或"进化"自己的知识|AI 永远是个读者，不是作者|
|❸|**盲盒检索 (Trigger Blindness)**：靠 cosine similarity 随机抽取。无法实现"当 X 发生时，想起 Y"这种条件触发|AI 的回忆是随机的，不是精确的|
|❹|**孤岛记忆 (Memory Islands)**：树结构只有纵向父子关系，向量空间只有模糊的余弦距离——A 节点提到了"某概念"，但系统无法自动发现 B 节点也在讨论同一概念|AI 的知识是碎片化的群岛，不是互联的大陆|
|❺|**无身份持久化 (No Identity Layer)**：RAG 没有"这条记忆比那条更重要"的概念，更没有"我是谁"的启动协议|每次启动，AI 都是陌生人|
|❻|**代理式记忆 (Proxy Memory)**：后台系统自动摘要对话内容，AI 自己不知道自己"记住了"什么，也无法决定"记什么"。记忆是第三人称的监控笔记，不是 AI 的思考产物|AI 是记忆的客体，不是主体|
**Nocturne Memory** 通过 Model Context Protocol (MCP) 协议，**逐条击破**上述缺陷：
|#|Nocturne Memory 的解法|对应 RAG 缺陷|
|❶|**🕸️ URI 图谱路由 (URI Graph Routing)**：记忆保持原始的层级结构（如 `core://agent/identity`、`project://architecture`）。路径本身就是语义，支持 Alias 别名构建多维关联网络。**不降维，不切碎。**|语义降维|
|❷|**✏️ 自主 CRUD + 版本控制 (Self-Evolving Memory)**：AI 可以 `create` / `update` / `delete` 自己的记忆。每次写入自动生成快照 (Snapshot)，人类 Owner 通过 Dashboard 一键审计、回滚或合并。|只读架构|
|❸|**🎯 条件触发路由 (Disclosure Routing)**：每条记忆绑定一个人类可读的触发条件（`disclosure`），如 *"当用户提到项目 X 时"*。AI 按当前情境精准注入，而非盲盒抽取。|盲盒检索|
|❹|**📖 豆辞典 (Glossary Auto-Hyperlinking)**：将关键词绑定到记忆节点（如 `"Salem"` → `core://my_user`）。任意记忆正文中出现该关键词时，系统通过 Aho-Corasick 多模式匹配自动检出并生成跨节点超链接。**写得越多，关联自动越密——记忆网络会自己织网。**|孤岛记忆|
|❺|**🧠 System Boot 身份协议**：用户在 Dashboard Settings 中配置 `Boot URIs` 列表，系统启动时通过 `system://boot` 自动加载这些核心记忆。AI 每次醒来都知道自己是谁、用户是谁、以及它的使命。**一次配置，永久唤醒。**|无身份持久化|
|❻|**🗡️ 第一人称主权记忆 (First-Person Sovereign Memory)**：没有后台自动摘要的系统。每一条记忆都由 AI 自己决定创建、组织和维护——以自身视角写下的认知产物，而非系统替它做的档案。**记忆属于写它的人，不属于监控它的系统。**|代理式记忆|

- **Muse** -- Meta Muse coding-plan quota tracking (5-hour prompts + weekly usage) from the same subscription snapshot `muse /usage` shows, via one minimal probe per poll. Opt-in: set `MUSE_ENABLED=true` and onWatch uses the key `muse login` stored (macOS Keychain / login file), or set `META_API_KEY` directly. Tracking stays off until you opt in, because each poll spends a prompt from your own 5h window. See Muse Setup.

- **Command Code** -- Credit balance plus the 5-hour and weekly rate-limit windows from the Command Code API, with billing-period cost, request and token totals. Auto-detected from the `cmd` CLI login (or the pi / OMP auth store); set `COMMAND_CODE_API_KEY` for Docker and headless hosts. Polling reads billing endpoints only, so it spends no credits. **Anthropic 429 rate limit errors:** Anthropic's `/api/oauth/usage` endpoint has aggressive rate limits (~5 requests per token). onWatch automatically handles this by refreshing the OAuth token when rate limited, which provides a fresh rate limit window. This is transparent to users - onWatch logs "Rate limit bypassed successfully" when this occurs. The workaround requires OAuth credentials (auto-detected from Claude Code); API key authentication does not support token refresh. See issue #16 and anthropics/claude-code#31021 for details.

The same code on Node 22.18+, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel, and the browser, with no native binaries on the `fetch`-based drivers.

- **Type-safe to the leaf, nothing to generate.** Every key is checked against your entity, down into populated relations and JSON/JSONB dot-paths, so `$like` on a numeric column is a compile error. No `.prisma` file, no generated client.

- **Decorators or plain data, your call.** An entity is a class with standard TC39 decorators, or plain data via `defineEntity`, its row type derived. Both are typed the same, mix in one project, and need no compiler flags or `reflect-metadata`.
- **Light.** Zero runtime dependencies and every dialect in one package, yet `uql-orm/postgres` is about 49 kB gzipped. See what we deleted to get there.

- **The hard things are built in.** Semantic and vector search, multi-tenant filters you cannot bypass by accident, soft-delete with restore, streaming, and drift checks that catch a database that no longer matches.
- **SQL when you need it.** `sql()` fits anywhere a value or a field goes, computed fields are SQL you can filter and sort on, and a migration can be plain SQL.

- **The fastest ORM.** On a full PostgreSQL round trip it adds the least over hand-written driver code of any ORM in our open-source benchmark, on Bun and Node alike. The same benchmark scores the types by compiling ordinary mistakes in each ORM's API: UQL is the only one that catches them all.

At the end of every batch the listener waits for the confirms of RabbitMQ (publisher confirms). `UseRabbitMq` therefore sets the batch size to 1,000 changes (the default of the library is 100). In our benchmark, with a durable queue bound to the exchange, the initial copy and the stream ran at about 31,000 rows per second with batches of 1,000, and at about 24,000 and 21,000 with batches of 100 (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ in Docker on the same machine). Larger batches added nothing: RabbitMQ itself used most of the CPU, routing and confirming every message, also when the messages were not persistent. For more throughput, use RabbitMQ Streams. To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseRabbitMq`. A batch that is not full is still confirmed after the batch wait time (100 ms by default).

The producer has up to one batch of messages in flight, and the listener waits for their confirmations at the end of the batch. `UseRabbitMqStreams` therefore sets the batch size to 10,000 changes (the default of the library is 100). In our benchmark the initial copy ran at about 170,000 rows per second and the stream at about 100,000 with batches of 10,000, and at about 68,000 and 42,000 with batches of 100 (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ in Docker on the same machine). To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseRabbitMqStreams`. A batch that is not full is still confirmed after the batch wait time (100 ms by default). After an error, the unconfirmed messages of the batch are sent again.

At the end of every batch the listener waits until Kafka has acknowledged all of its messages (with `acks=all`, which idempotence needs). `UseKafka` therefore sets the batch size to 10,000 changes (the default of the library is 100). In our benchmark the initial copy ran at about 140,000 rows per second and the stream at about 94,000 with batches of 10,000, and at about 8,800 and 8,300 with batches of 100 (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and Kafka in Docker on the same machine). The batching of librdkafka itself (`linger.ms`, 5 ms by default) made no difference there. To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseKafka`. A batch that is not full is still confirmed after the batch wait time (100 ms by default). After an error, the unconfirmed messages of the batch are sent again.

Every batch of changes is one transaction. `UseSqlite` sets the batch size to 1,000 changes (the default of the library is 100). In our benchmark with batches of 1,000 and the database file on the server's disk, the initial copy ran at about 55,000 rows per second and the stream at about 50,000, or about 68,000 and 61,000 with `options.UseWal = true` (the WAL journal mode of SQLite), since a commit then waits less for the disk. With the file in memory (tmpfs), where a commit does not wait for a disk, they ran at about 85,000 and 75,000 (with or without `UseWal`), and at about 72,000 and 68,000 with batches of 100 (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs, 8 GB RAM and its local disk with ext4, with PostgreSQL in Docker on the same machine). Larger batches add little. To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseSqlite`. A batch that is not full is still written after the batch wait time (100 ms by default).

Every batch of changes is written with `BatchWriteItem` requests of up to 25 items, and `MaxParallelBatchWrites` of them (8 by default) are in flight at a time. Two changes of the same row are never in flight together, so they are applied in order. The position is saved once per batch, after its rows. `UseDynamoDb` sets the batch size to 1,000 changes (the default of the library is 100), so that the parallel requests have work. In our benchmark, against DynamoDB Local, 8 parallel requests were about 2.5 times faster than one (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and DynamoDB Local in Docker on the same machine). DynamoDB Local is not DynamoDB: on AWS the throughput depends on the network and on the capacity of the tables, so measure it with your own tables (`--dynamodb URL`). To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseDynamoDb`. A batch that is not full is still written after the batch wait time (100 ms by default).
Note that this is not fully standard compliant. It can only be used for idempotency check if the `BatchSize` is 1.
Otherwise, deduplication keys from the individual messages should be used.

Every batch of changes is one POST, and the listener waits for its answer before it goes on. The batch size is the default of the library, 100 changes. In our benchmark, with a webhook that only reads the request, the initial copy ran at about 130,000 rows per second and the stream at about 81,000 with batches of 100, at about 184,000 and 86,000 with batches of 1,000, and at about 209,000 and 106,000 with batches of 10,000 (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL in Docker on the same machine and the webhook in the process of the benchmark). A larger batch is a larger request (about 300 bytes a row in the benchmark), so call `WithBatchSize` after `UseWebhook` if your webhook takes it. A batch that is not full is still sent after the batch wait time (100 ms by default).

The output uses the HTTP interface of ClickHouse, and sends the rows as JSON, or in the faster RowBinary format if you turn it on (see Insert format). It needs no ClickHouse client library, and is tested with ClickHouse 26.10.
- `_version`: the position of the change in the PostgreSQL WAL (`w * 2^64 + n` of the deduplication key). A copied row has version 0.

- A table that already exists is used as it is. To choose the column types or an engine the options do not offer (for example a replicated one), create the table before the first row arrives. It needs the columns `_version UInt128` and `_deleted UInt8`. With RowBinary, a column type it does not cover makes the rows of the table go as JSON: see Insert format.

- `PartitionBy`: a `PARTITION BY` expression. The default is no partitions. The cleanup of deleted rows works per partition: a partition that has had no new rows (inserts, updates or deletes) for that long is cleaned up, even while other partitions of the table get new rows.
- `ReplacingMergeTree` (the default) keeps the latest version of every row.

- `MergeTree` keeps every version, deletes included: the history of the table, in the order of `_version`. Read it without `FINAL`. A change that PostgreSQL replays after a reconnect is there twice, with the same `_version`.

- `Null` keeps nothing: only the materialized views on the table get the rows. An update that did not change a large value has `null` for it, because there is no row to take it from, unless the table has `REPLICA IDENTITY FULL`.

ClickHouse wants few, large inserts. `UseClickHouse` therefore sets the batch size to 10,000 changes (the default of the library is 100). In our benchmark the initial copy ran at about 1,500 rows per second with batches of 100 and at about 95,000 with batches of 10,000, or about 105,000 with RowBinary (see Insert format) (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and ClickHouse in Docker on the same machine). To use another size, call `WithBatchSize` after `UseClickHouse`. A batch that is not full is still sent after the batch wait time (100 ms by default).

With `options.UseRowBinary = true` they are sent in RowBinary, which ClickHouse reads two to three times faster (measured on a Hetzner CX33, a cost-optimized cloud server with 4 shared vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, with PostgreSQL and ClickHouse in Docker on the same machine). In our benchmark it made the initial copy and the stream about 10% faster on the same machine, since the inserts are only a part of the time. It is newer, and off by default, as the binary format of PostgreSQL's own replication: the output then does what the parser of ClickHouse does with the text (the time zone of a `timestamp`, dates out of range, decimal digits), so a difference would be stored without an error.

- `server --with-gateway` also runs a gateway instance in the same process. Each replica joins the system pool `local` of the first organization (by creation time) with a system join token (max uses 1); before `Setup` it checks for an organization every 5s. It reaches its own server over loopback (`http://127.0.0.1:<WERBOT_HTTP_ADDR port>`, tunnel `https://127.0.0.1:<WERBOT_GATEWAY_ADDR port>`), so both addresses must accept connections on 127.0.0.1: leave the host empty (`:8080`) or use `0.0.0.0` or `127.0.0.1`, not a single non-loopback IP. It keeps its identity in `WERBOT_DATA_DIR/gateway` (or `WERBOT_GATEWAY_DATA_DIR`) and reads the other `WERBOT_GATEWAY_*` variables (docs/configuration.md); it refuses loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata), multicast and unspecified targets and the resolved addresses of the database host unless `WERBOT_LOCAL_POOL_ALLOW_LOOPBACK=true` (docs/configuration.md), so a same-host database needs that opt-in, while the host's LAN addresses stay reachable (this applies to `telnet`, `tcp` and `udp` sessions and to health probes; `ssh` resources keep their own dial, so a loopback `ssh` resource connects but its health shows `unhealthy`); its metrics go to the server's `/metrics`. Database and enrollment errors before the instance is enrolled are logged and retried (the wait doubles up to 5 minutes, a new system token each time); a busy SSH port or a failure after enrollment stops the server. On shutdown the gateway drains its sessions before the server closes the tunnel, so allow `WERBOT_GATEWAY_DRAIN_TIMEOUT` plus about 40s for the stop (compose: `stop_grace_period: 70s`).

- `connect` opens local ports that reach `tcp`, `udp` and other port resources through a gateway (docs/connect.md); `connect --vnet` gives each resource an address and a name `<resource>.<org>.werbot` instead (Linux and macOS, root or `CAP_NET_ADMIN`; docs/vnet.md).
- `request`, `requests`, `approve`, `deny` ask for just-in-time access to a resource, list requests and decide them (docs/cli.md); `ls` marks resources you can only request with `ACCESS` `request`.

- `login`, `logout`, `status`, `ls`, `ssh`, `ssh-config` sign the CLI in with a browser or device flow, keep a profile and a short-lived SSH certificate in `WERBOT_HOME`, and open sessions with the system `ssh` (docs/cli.md); `connect` uses the profile when there is one. `proxy` connects stdin and stdout to a gateway (over SSH or its WebSocket URL) for an OpenSSH `ProxyCommand`.
- `mcp`, `agent run`, `agents` run an AI agent as a run of your account (MCP on stdio, or a program with `ssh` set up) and manage your agents and agent profiles (docs/agents.md).

- `ApprovalPolicyService` (owners and admins): approval policies that say who may request access to which resources, who approves and how (`manual` or `auto`, `max_duration`, `require_reason`, `four_eyes`, `break_glass`) (docs/jit.md).

- `AccessRequestService` (every member): access requests, approvals, grants and break-glass reviews. Nobody approves their own request, and a pending request that times out is `expired`, never approved (docs/jit.md).

- `LockService` (owners and admins): locks on a user, team, resource, grant, CLI session, agent, agent run, the agents of a user or all agents; a lock beats every binding and grant and ends matching sessions within 2 s (docs/jit.md).

- Organization settings (owners and admins, web UI `/settings`): CLI session lifetimes, grant and request lengths, `lock_mode` and `mask_output` (`agents` by default, `all` or `none`: whose exec output the gateway masks) (docs/jit.md).

- `PolicyService` command policies (owners and admins, web UI `/policies/commands` and `/policies/custom`): the gateway sorts each exec command into risk classes, and class overrides, command rules (`deny` or `approval`) and custom Cedar policies decide it; a command under `approval` waits until an approver decides on `/requests`. Details: docs/policies.md.

- `PolicyService` folder and terminal rules (owners and admins, web UI `/policies/paths` and `/policies/terminal`): folder rules limit the paths a command may touch, and terminal rules open interactive shells as a command console that checks every line, or refuse them (docs/policies.md).

- `AgentService`, `AgentProfileService` (web UI `/agents`): agents with their limits and status, runs with their timeline (tool calls, sessions, approvals, denials), resume and end, and agent profiles for another OS user or a container (docs/agents.md).

- `IdentityProviderService` (owners and admins, web UI `/settings/sso`): OpenID Connect single sign-on with claims mapping to teams and roles, verified-email linking and an hourly IdP check that ends sessions of users the IdP refused (docs/sso.md).

- `MFAService`, `MFAChallengeService` (web UI `/profile/mfa`, `/policies/mfa`): TOTP, passkeys and recovery codes; `require_mfa` off, admins or all; MFA rules that ask a second factor on SSH and in the web terminal; fresh MFA for admin actions; rate limits on login, password reset, MFA and the token endpoint (docs/mfa.md).

- Web terminal and live view (web UI buttons **Open terminal**, **Watch**, **Terminate**): WebSockets `GET /api/terminal?resource=<name>&cols=&rows=` and `GET /api/sessions/{id}/live`, only with a session (cookie or a person's CLI token) and the `Origin` of `WERBOT_WEB_URL`, never for agent tokens. The terminal goes through the gateway like SSH (same access rules, recording and audit, `front: web`); the live view is read-only and audited as `session.observe`. Server replicas bridge streams over the mTLS listener `WERBOT_INTERNAL_ADDR` (default `:8444`). Details, close codes and limits: docs/web-terminal.md.

- `geoip.refresh` (on start, then daily at 04:00 UTC) downloads the monthly country database from `WERBOT_GEOIP_URL`, by default DB-IP Country Lite from `download.db-ip.com`; MaxMind GeoLite2 and IPinfo Lite also work (configuration.md). The database is stored in Postgres (no files on disk), and every server loads it on start. Without it, country rules deny. IP geolocation by DB-IP (default database).

Oxigraph is an excellent Rust SPARQL database. It stores data in RocksDB, which needs a native storage engine and a local filesystem. That rules it out in exactly the places where many modern apps run:

|**Hash ids computed in Rust.** Each term becomes a tagged 64-bit integer (xxh3).|Writes never read anything back. SPARQL constants become integer literals at compile time, with no dictionary lookup.|
|**Inline values.** Canonical integers and booleans live inside the id, and integer ids sort by value.|`FILTER(?age > 30)` on inline integers needs no join, and ranges become id ranges.|

|**Covering `WITHOUT ROWID` indexes.** `quads` is clustered on `spog`, with `posg`, `ospg` and an optional `gspo`.|Every triple-pattern scan is index-only. Only 3–4 B-trees are written per quad, which matters because D1 bills every index entry.|

|**One SQL statement per query.** Joins, OPTIONAL, UNION, MINUS, aggregates, property paths (recursive CTEs) and ORDER BY/LIMIT all compile into a single `SELECT`.|On D1 each round-trip is milliseconds. A query costs 1–2 round-trips, not one per triple pattern or per row.|

|**Our own join ordering.** Per-predicate and per-class statistics drive a greedy planner, enforced with `CROSS JOIN`.|SQLite's planner can't tell `rdf:type` from a rare predicate in an N-way self-join. Choosing the order ourselves avoids scans that are 1000× too large.|
|**Typed side columns.** `num`, `nt` and `ts` columns (with partial indexes) sit on the term dictionary.|Numeric and date comparisons never re-parse lexical forms.|

|**Atomic = one batch.** Every write, including `DELETE/INSERT … WHERE`, compiles to self-reading SQL that fits in one transaction.|D1 has no interactive transactions; `batch()` is its only atomic unit.|
The full rationale is in `lat.md/decisions.md` and `lat.md/architecture.md`.

|**Oxigraph 0.5 family**: `oxrdf`, `oxrdfio`/`oxttl`, `spargebra`, `sparesults`, `oxsdatatypes`, `spareval`|Data model, all RDF parsers and serializers, the SPARQL parser and algebra, result formats, XSD datatypes, and a fallback evaluator for anything the SQL compiler can't express|
|**rudof**: `srdf`, `shacl_validation`, `shex_validation`|SHACL and ShEx validation over the store (same Oxigraph crate family, so no conversions)|

|No extensions or user-defined functions|Every SPARQL function has a pure-SQL form or a rewrite. The few that don't (general `REGEX`, `REPLACE`, hashes) return a clear "unsupported on this backend" error, and `explain()` flags them.|

|No interactive transactions; `batch()` is the only atomic unit|Every write is one batch. `DELETE/INSERT … WHERE` stages its WHERE results in `update_buffer` inside the same batch, so SPARQL's evaluate-then-apply semantics hold.|

|Statement size limit (100 KB), 100 bound parameters, 50 statements per batch|Constants are inlined as escaped SQL literals and never bound. Generated SQL is kept under 90 KB (larger queries report `unsupported`), and large inserts are split into statements and batches under the limits.|

|Parser limits: at most 5 terms in a compound SELECT, GLOB patterns up to 50 bytes|Large UNIONs are nested into groups of at most five, and lexical-form checks split their GLOB patterns into short pieces.|
|JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53|Ids (60-bit) are selected as TEXT and parsed in the core.|
|Billed per row read and written|Few indexes, read-free writes, no per-write statistics updates, one statement per query, and deduplicated term resolution.|
|Per-invocation query limits|Queries use 1–2 requests; bulk loads are chunked (and documented as non-atomic across chunks, like Oxigraph's `BulkLoader`).|

- **Schema registry.** A named graph can be declared to hold an ontology, a SHACL shapes graph or a ShEx schema, and mapped to the data graphs it applies to. Its triples stay ordinary RDF, but reasoning then reads only the active ontologies that apply to each graph, SHACL shapes are compiled into an index that Cypher and rudof both read, and `QueryOptions::include_schema_graphs = false` keeps axioms out of queries over the data. The registry is itself RDF, in the system graph `<oxilite:schema>`, described with the `oxl:` vocabulary and checked by its own SHACL shapes: SPARQL can read and change it, it survives an N-Quads dump, and the same updates run on Oxigraph. A store that registers nothing is unchanged. Reference: `docs/schema-registry.md`.

- **Coverage.** 3733 of the 3880 openCypher TCK scenarios pass (read-only 96.4%, temporal functions 100%), on the bundled SQLite; the failures (user-defined procedures, reading after a write in one statement, errors on deleted entities…) are listed in `crates/oxilite-cypher/tck-allowlist.txt`.

oxilite stores JSON-LD documents and W3C Verifiable Credentials as they are, and makes their RDF queryable (features `jsonld` and `vc`, crates `oxilite-jsonld` and `oxilite-vc`). Each document is kept **byte for byte** in a keyed table, and its RDF goes into a **named graph of its own**. By default the key and the graph are both the document's `id`, so a credential is found under its own IRI in both.

- **Standard JSON-LD.** Conversion uses the `json-ld` crate: 450 tests of the W3C JSON-LD 1.1 `toRdf` suite pass (4 allow-listed crate limitations). Contexts load offline. Register them in memory, or persist them in the store with `putContext`. Network loading is opt-in, and Node-only on the JavaScript side.
